g9-geography-ug6-t1.overview: Humans and the environment shape each other constantly. This lesson explains the three modes of interaction - dependence, modification and adaptation - and the two main types of human links with the environment: resource use and waste production.
objectives: Define environment and describe the human-environment relationship
Identify the three modes of human-environment interaction
Explain how humans affect the physical environment and vice versa
Group human-environment links into resource use and waste production
Give Ethiopian examples of resource use such as forests, energy and water
g9-geography-ug6-t1.simple: Environment means our physical surroundings and the characteristics of the place where we live, including the land, sea and atmosphere. Humans depend on the environment for air, water, food, shelter and energy; they modify it by cutting forests, building homes and farming; and they adapt to it, as people living in deserts and cold regions show. The links between human activity and the environment fall into two main types: use of natural resources such as land, water, soils and minerals, and production of wastes from agriculture, industry and daily life. In Ethiopia, clearing forest for farming and fuel, generating hydroelectric power and polluting water bodies all show this interaction clearly.
g9-geography-ug6-t1.detailed:
What environment means. Environment refers to the physical surroundings and the characteristics of the place in which we live, and also to the wider natural world of land, sea and atmosphere. Humans have interacted with their environment since they began to live on the Earth: for centuries people have cut forests to grow crops, altering the environment, while the environment affects humans too - we change our clothes in response to cold or hot weather.

Three modes of interaction. The relationship between humans and the environment can be seen in three ways: dependence, modification and adaptation. Dependence means every living thing relies on its environment for air, water, food or shelter. Modification means human activities frequently change the environment, both negatively and positively - even sustainable farming and renewable energy projects use resources from nature, and people build homes, shopping centers and schools on land. Adaptation means people live even in the Arctic, deserts and dense forest regions because of increased knowledge of the environment; the more successfully a species adapts, the more likely it is to survive.

The environment acts on people. A good climate, accessible clean water and fertile soil enable people to live and thrive, while harsh environments - very hot or cold climate, limited water, infertile land - make survival difficult. Environmental events such as earthquakes, floods and drought damage homes, property and agriculture, displace people, destroy livelihoods, and can damage water sources and pipelines, causing contamination and spreading waterborne diseases.

Two main types of links. The links between human activities and the environment are grouped into two: use of natural resources such as land, food, water, soils, minerals, plants and animals; and production of wastes from activities including agriculture, industry and mining, as well as wastes from our bodies.

Use of forest resources. Globally, both population and resource extraction increased by almost 50 percent in the 25 years from 1980 to 2005, and world population rose from 4.44 billion in 1980 to 7.8 billion in 2020. In Ethiopia, clearing land for agriculture to meet food needs and the demand for fuel and construction materials has caused a steady loss of forest area. Deforestation reduces biodiversity, the measure of the variety of living organisms, yet we rely on other organisms for food (fish, goats, wheat, maize), medicines, and ecological services such as providing oxygen, purifying water and controlling erosion. Removing trees is also a contributory cause of soil erosion: without roots binding the soil and vegetation intercepting rain, soil is washed away, and lower soil permeability reduces groundwater recharge.

Energy and water resources. Fossil fuels powered global industrialization but are non-renewable and their burning is the main cause of climate change. In Ethiopia, wind farms generate electricity, but the most important renewable source is water: the country has several hydroelectric power stations and more are planned, including the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam. Solar power using photovoltaic cells is another renewable option. Water is used directly for domestic purposes (drinking, washing, cooking), agriculture (irrigation) and industry; globally agriculture is the biggest user. Countries with less than 1700 cubic meters of water per person per year are water stressed, and those with less than 1000 cubic meters are water scarce.

Waste and pollution. Pollution means the introduction into the environment of substances liable to harm humans and other living organisms. The leather industry produces liquid wastes from tanning containing organic materials and toxic chemicals including known human carcinogens. Burning fuels releases greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide, which cause human-induced climate change. Open defecation and inadequate sanitation spread waterborne diseases caused by pathogens in contaminated water and food.

keyTerms.def: The physical surroundings and characteristics of the place we live, and the wider natural world of land, sea and atmosphere.
The mode of interaction in which living beings rely on the environment for air, water, food and shelter.
Changing the environment through human activities, with both negative and positive results.
Adjusting to environmental conditions, which allows humans to live in regions such as deserts, forests and cold areas.
A measure of the variety of living organisms in an area.
All living organisms and their physical environment, together with the interactions between them.
Catching fish at a faster rate than they can reproduce, a form of over-exploitation.
The introduction into the environment of substances liable to cause harm to humans and other living organisms.
The condition of a country with less than 1700 cubic meters of water per person per year for all purposes.

workedExamples.problem: Global population grew from 4.44 billion in 1980 to 7.8 billion in 2020. What does this trend imply for natural resource extraction?
workedExamples.given: World population rose from 4.44 billion (1980) to 7.8 billion (2020); population and resource extraction each rose almost 50 percent during 1980 to 2005.
workedExamples.formula: Concept: more people need more resources, so population growth drives resource extraction upward.
workedExamples.substitution: Population increased by about 3.36 billion over 40 years, while extraction already matched population growth between 1980 and 2005.
workedExamples.calculation: Since consumption per person also rises with socio-economic progress, total demand grows faster than population alone, explaining the steady rise in extraction with the greatest amounts in the most recent years.
workedExamples.answer: Rapid population growth and rising per-person consumption together cause a steady increase in global resource extraction.

workedExamples.problem: Country A provides 1400 cubic meters of water per person per year and Country B provides 950 cubic meters. Classify both using the textbook figures.
workedExamples.given: Water stress threshold: less than 1700 cubic meters per person per year. Water scarcity threshold: less than 1000 cubic meters per person per year.
workedExamples.formula: Method: compare per-person water availability against the two threshold figures.
workedExamples.substitution: A: 1400 is below 1700 but above 1000. B: 950 is below 1000.
workedExamples.calculation: A falls between the two thresholds, so it is water stressed; B falls below the lower threshold, so it is water scarce.
workedExamples.answer: Country A is water stressed and Country B is water scarce.

workedExamples.problem: Fishermen using small boats catch few fish, while modern industrial fleets cover huge areas of ocean and catch far more. What is the geographic consequence?
workedExamples.given: Technology lets fleets fish at greater depths over huge areas; fish stocks reproduce at a fixed natural rate.
workedExamples.formula: Concept: advanced technology increases exploitation per capita and can exceed the rate of reproduction.
workedExamples.substitution: Catching exceeds the reproduction rate of fish populations.
workedExamples.calculation: When removal is faster than reproduction, stocks shrink and the wider ecosystem loses a component, producing knock-on effects on other parts of the system.
workedExamples.answer: Overfishing, which can damage or destroy entire ecosystems.

workedExamples.problem: A farmer clears forest for cropland. Using the textbook, predict the chain of environmental consequences.
workedExamples.given: Trees and undergrowth are removed and not replanted; roots previously bound the soil and intercepted rainfall.
workedExamples.formula: Concept: vegetation loss removes soil binding, interception and deep root channels for water recharge.
workedExamples.substitution: Exposed ground plus no binding roots plus unblocked rainfall runoff.
workedExamples.calculation: Rain washes away exposed soil (erosion), biodiversity falls, and reduced permeability cuts the rainwater soaking in to replenish groundwater.
workedExamples.answer: Deforestation leads to soil erosion, biodiversity loss, reduced groundwater recharge and loss of forest habitats.

commonMistakes: Thinking the environment only influences people and forgetting that humans also change the environment.
Confusing adaptation with modification; adapting means adjusting to conditions, modifying means changing the environment itself.
Believing humans are no longer dependent on the environment because of modern technology.
Assuming renewable energy is completely impact-free; even wood fuel causes deforestation.
Mixing up water stress (less than 1700 cubic meters) with water scarcity (less than 1000 cubic meters).
Thinking resource growth is caused only by more people and ignoring rising consumption per person.
applications: Tracing the resources behind a school notebook: wood, water, energy, soil and land for the trees.
Observing how your locality depends on a nearby river, farmland or forest for daily needs.
Explaining why Ethiopia builds hydropower stations such as the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam instead of relying only on fossil fuels.
Listing the three water uses in your home: drinking and washing, irrigation, and industry.
Identifying in your town where wastes from households, leather industries or transport enter air, water and soil.
g9-geography-ug6-t1.summary: Humans and the environment interact through dependence, modification and adaptation, and these links consist of using natural resources and producing wastes. Ethiopia's forest clearing, hydropower development and water use show both sides of the relationship. Because resources are finite, mismanaging this interaction causes erosion, biodiversity loss and pollution.

g9-geography-ug6-t2.overview: Optimum population is the ideal balance between a country's people and its resources. This lesson defines optimum population, lists its indications, and shows the link between optimal population and sustainable development.
objectives: Define optimum population and the highest quality of life it brings
State the indications that a population is near the optimum
Explain how optimum population yields the highest income per capita
Describe the factors that make optima vary in time and space
Demonstrate a balanced relationship between population size and resource use
g9-geography-ug6-t2.simple: Optimum population exists when the resources available in a country are equal to its population's needs, so there are enough resources to maintain everyone. It is the best and most desirable size of a country's population. With the existing natural resources and a given level of technology, the optimum population yields the highest income per capita and the highest quality of life: every person has adequate food, water, energy and clean air, medical care, recreation and cultural outlets. Signs of optimum population include high living standards, full employment, rational use of increasing resources and a balanced population structure. The optimum is not fixed - it changes with geography, technology and social conditions.
g9-geography-ug6-t2.detailed:
Definition. Optimum population is where the amount of resources available in a country is equal to the country's population needs, so there are enough resources to maintain its population. It means the best and the most desirable size of a country's population, neither too many people nor too few.

Quality of life and income. Optimum population yields the highest quality of life, meaning each person has access to adequate food, water, energy and air of the highest quality, adequate medical care, recreational facilities and cultural outlets. It is also defined as the population size which, along with the existing natural resources and a given state of technology, yields the highest income per capita in a country.

Indications of optimum population. The signs are high average living standards, full employment, rational development of increasing resources and a balanced demographic structure, but these are not precise criteria; they help us recognise an optimum without measuring it exactly.

Optima vary in time and space. The optimum size changes according to a wide variety of factors: the size of a state, its geography, its social structure, its stage of technical progress and the quality of communications. In general, the numerical range of the optimum is greater in varied economies and open environments than in specialized economies and isolated communities, where population growth, economic crises, war or drought can prove disastrous to the delicate balance between population and resources.

Link to sustainable development. When population and resources are in balance, resources are used rationally and are maintained for the future, so development can continue over time. If a locality's population and resources were at an optimum level, we would expect water, forest, soil and farmland to be used at rates they can replenish, with no shortage and no degradation.

keyTerms.def: The population size at which a country's available resources equal its population's needs, giving the highest income per capita and quality of life.
Access to adequate food, water, energy, clean air, medical care, recreation and cultural outlets.
The average income of each person in a country; it is highest at the optimum population.
A condition in which nearly everyone who wants work can find it; an indication of optimum population.
A population age and sex composition that is not distorted, one indication of an optimal population.
The maximum population an area's resources can support at a given standard of living.
Development that meets present needs without destroying the resources needed by future generations.
Using resources prudently so they increase or renew rather than being wasted.

workedExamples.problem: A country of 60 million people has farmland, water and energy exactly sufficient to feed, employ and support all of them at good living standards. Identify the population concept and justify it.
workedExamples.given: Population 60 million; resources equal to the population's needs; living standards high; employment broad.
workedExamples.formula: Concept: optimum population is where available resources equal population needs.
workedExamples.substitution: Resources available = population needs for 60 million people.
workedExamples.calculation: Since needs are met fully and resources are neither short nor idle, the population sits at the ideal size, with income per capita maximized for the given technology.
workedExamples.answer: This is optimum population, the most desirable size giving the highest quality of life.

workedExamples.problem: A geographer observes a country with high average living standards, full employment, expanding but rationally used resources and a balanced demographic structure. What can be concluded?
workedExamples.given: All four textbook indications of optimum population are present.
workedExamples.formula: Method: check observed conditions against the textbook list of indications.
workedExamples.substitution: High living standards - present; full employment - present; rational resource development - present; balanced demographic structure - present.
workedExamples.calculation: Although the indications are not precise criteria, their full presence strongly suggests the population is close to its optimum for existing resources and technology.
workedExamples.answer: The country is likely at or near its optimum population.

workedExamples.problem: Two countries have identical resource endowments but one has advanced technical progress and good communications while the other is an isolated, specialized economy far from markets. Which has the wider optimum range?
workedExamples.given: Same resources; differing structures: varied open economy versus specialized isolated community.
workedExamples.formula: Concept: the optimal band is wider in varied economies and open environments than in specialized or isolated ones.
workedExamples.substitution: Country A is varied and open; Country B is specialized and isolated.
workedExamples.calculation: In B, population growth, economic crises, war or drought can be disastrous because the narrow economy offers little flexibility; A can absorb shocks and support a wider range of population sizes.
workedExamples.answer: Country A has the wider numerical range of optimum population.

commonMistakes: Thinking optimum population means the largest possible population a country can cram in.
Believing the optimum is a fixed number that never changes; it varies with technology, geography and social structure.
Assuming one strict formula defines the optimum; the textbook says the criteria are not precise.
Confusing optimum population with overpopulation, where people already exceed resources.
Forgetting that optimum population depends on the given state of technology, which can raise it over time.
Thinking optimum population guarantees wealth for every individual regardless of distribution.
applications: Judging whether your woreda's farmland, water and forest match its population size.
Explaining why new irrigation technology or better roads can raise a region's optimum population.
Debating that protecting natural resources today keeps the population-resource balance for future citizens.
Using the four indications to discuss where Ethiopia stands relative to its own resource base.
Predicting how drought or conflict could upset a delicate population-resource balance in an isolated community.
g9-geography-ug6-t2.summary: Optimum population is the most desirable size where a country's resources equal its people's needs, yielding the highest income per capita and quality of life. Its indications are high living standards, full employment, rational resource development and a balanced demographic structure. Because the optimum shifts with state size, geography, technology and communications, countries should keep resources healthy so the balance lasts.

g9-geography-ug6-t3.overview: Overpopulation occurs when people exceed the resources available to them. This lesson defines overpopulation, separates its absolute and relative forms, and explains its causes and wide-ranging effects.
objectives: Define overpopulation and state when it occurs
Distinguish absolute from relative overpopulation
Identify the causes of rural and industrial overpopulation
Explain how population growth affects resource availability
Assess the environmental and socio-economic effects of overpopulation
g9-geography-ug6-t3.simple: Overpopulation occurs when there is an excess of population over utilized or potential resources. It can result from a rising population, declining resources, a falling demand for labor, or a combination of these. Absolute overpopulation happens when the limit of production is reached while living standards stay low; relative overpopulation means production could be increased but is not - and relative is more common. Overpopulation appears at rural, industrial, regional and national levels. It is caused by more births, falling mortality, immigration, lack of education and poverty. Its effects include resource depletion, water shortages, pollution, deforestation, soil erosion, global warming, loss of arable land, migration, malnutrition, low life expectancy, high crime and conflict over scarce resources.
g9-geography-ug6-t3.detailed:
Definition and causes. Overpopulation occurs when there is an excess of population over utilized or potential resources. It may result from an increase in population, a decline in resources, a decline in the demand for labor, or a combination. It can arise where resource development does not keep pace with population growth, or where growth of tertiary services lags behind technical progress. It can also stem from an increase in births, a fall in mortality due to medical advances, increased immigration and decreased emigration, lack of education, poverty and poor contraceptive use.

Absolute and relative overpopulation. Absolute overpopulation occurs where the absolute limit of production has been attained though living standards remain low. Relative overpopulation means present production is inadequate for the population although greater production is feasible; it is more common than the absolute form. Invariably, overpopulation expresses itself at the lowest levels of society: rural overpopulation affects the landless and smallholders, while industrial overpopulation hits unskilled and semi-skilled workers.

Levels and regional patterns. Overpopulation may be found at rural, industrial, regional and national levels. Rural overpopulation is common and most striking in populous underdeveloped areas. In South-East Asia, with high fertility, declining mortality, intensive agriculture, land fragmentation and minimal mechanization, natural checks historically exercised great control. The demographic evolution of China has been frequently interrupted by famines, floods, droughts and epidemics.

How rural overpopulation arises. The four textbook causes are: uneven distribution of land among farmers; increased mechanization reducing demand for agricultural laborers; a change from cultivation to livestock farming, again reducing labor demand; and rapid rural population growth. Similar features appear in old countries of Europe, where famine, hunger, prolonged unemployment, and growth of landless laborers and beggars were symptoms of rural overpopulation. Solutions other than emigration are slow and difficult, but in the long run social and cultural revolutions are more effective.

Effects. Overpopulation depletes resources, especially fossil fuels, and causes water shortages, increased air pollution, water pollution, soil erosion and noise pollution, deforestation and loss of ecosystems, changes in atmospheric composition and consequent global warming, permanent loss of arable land, and increases in desertification. It drives migration, mass species extinctions, starvation, malnutrition or poor diet with diet-deficiency diseases such as rickets, low life expectancy, a high crime rate, and conflict over scarce resources. It also over-utilizes infrastructure such as mass transit, highways and public health systems, and pushes land prices up.

keyTerms.def: An excess of population over the utilized or potential resources of an area.
Overpopulation at which the absolute limit of production has been reached while living standards remain low.
Overpopulation where present production is inadequate but greater production is feasible; more common than absolute.
Excess population in the countryside relative to land and agricultural labor opportunities.
Excess urban workers relative to jobs, hitting the unskilled and semi-skilled hardest.
Dividing farmland into increasingly small plots among farming families, typical of overpopulated rural areas.
The number of people an area's resources can support; overpopulation numbers exceed it.
The spread of desert-like conditions through land degradation, increased by overpopulation pressure.
A diet-deficiency disease (vitamin D or calcium deficiency) cited as a consequence of overpopulation-driven poverty.

workedExamples.problem: Region A can no longer increase production using any available means, yet most people remain poor. Region B produces far less than its land, water and skills could yield. Classify both.
workedExamples.given: A: production at its absolute limit, low living standards. B: production inadequate but expansion feasible.
workedExamples.formula: Concept: absolute overpopulation means the production limit is reached; relative overpopulation means output could rise but has not.
workedExamples.substitution: A shows a production limit, so it is absolute; B shows unused potential, so it is relative.
workedExamples.calculation: The textbook states relative overpopulation is more common than absolute, and B's unused potential fits that form.
workedExamples.answer: A shows absolute overpopulation; B shows relative overpopulation, the more common type.

workedExamples.problem: In a rural district, tractors replace hand labor, some farmers shift entirely to livestock, and land holdings are very unequal while the population grows quickly. Why is unemployment rising?
workedExamples.given: Mechanization, a shift from cultivation to livestock, uneven land distribution and rapid rural growth are all observed.
workedExamples.formula: Concept: the four textbook causes of rural overpopulation reduce demand for agricultural labor.
workedExamples.substitution: Mechanization cuts labor demand; livestock farming cuts it further; unequal land leaves many landless; rapid growth adds more workers every year.
workedExamples.calculation: Fewer jobs combined with more job seekers produces an excess of rural people over available opportunities and land.
workedExamples.answer: Rural overpopulation: population exceeds the land and labor opportunities available, so unemployment, landlessness and poverty grow.

workedExamples.problem: A country's births rise while medical advances cut death rates, immigrants arrive, and many people lack education. Predict resource consequences.
workedExamples.given: Rising births, falling mortality, increased immigration, lack of education represent textbook causes of overpopulation.
workedExamples.formula: Concept: overpopulation depletes resources and degrades the environment.
workedExamples.substitution: Population pressure rises on fuels, water, forests, soil and transport systems.
workedExamples.calculation: Expect fossil fuel depletion, water shortages, air, water, soil and noise pollution, deforestation, permanent loss of arable land, desertification and conflict as demand grows faster than supply.
workedExamples.answer: Resource depletion and widespread environmental degradation along with social problems such as low life expectancy and conflict.

workedExamples.problem: Why does the textbook say overpopulation invariably hits the lowest levels of society hardest? Argue with evidence.
workedExamples.given: Overpopulation appears at rural, industrial, regional and national levels.
workedExamples.formula: Concept: impacts fall on the least protected groups first.
workedExamples.substitution: Rural overpopulation best hits the landless and smallholders; industrial overpopulation best hits unskilled and semi-skilled workers.
workedExamples.calculation: Because these groups lack land, skills or savings to buffer shortages, famine, prolonged unemployment and loss of income reach them first.
workedExamples.answer: The landless, smallholders and unskilled urban workers absorb the impacts of overpopulation before anyone else.

commonMistakes: Believing overpopulation means a country simply has many people, regardless of its resources.
Confusing absolute and relative overpopulation; absolute is the rare reached-limit case.
Thinking overpopulation affects all social classes equally; it strikes hardest at the lowest levels.
Forgetting that overpopulation can result from declining resources or falling labor demand, not only from more births.
Listing only environmental effects and ignoring social effects like crime, migration and conflict.
Assuming emigration is the only solution; the textbook says social and cultural changes work better in the long run.
applications: Debating whether Ethiopia is overpopulated by comparing population growth with resource development.
Explaining why land in crowded rural highlands is divided into ever smaller plots among heirs.
Linking rapid urban growth in Addis Ababa to pressure on housing, mass transit and land prices.
Showing how a decline in resources, such as drying water points, can create overpopulation without any rise in births.
Identifying which local group suffers first when jobs and land run short: the landless and the unskilled.
g9-geography-ug6-t3.summary: Overpopulation is an excess of population over utilized or potential resources; it is usually relative, meaning output could expand but has not, rather than absolute. It originates in rising births, falling mortality, migration, poverty and low education, and it scars both environment and society - depleting fuels, fouling air and water, driving deforestation, soil erosion, desertification, migration, malnutrition and conflict.

g9-geography-ug6-t4.overview: Underpopulation exists when an area's people are too few to use its resources fully. This lesson defines underpopulation, shows why it is uncommon in its absolute form, and weighs its advantages and disadvantages for resource use.
objectives: Define underpopulation and state when it exists
Distinguish absolute from relative under-population
Describe the characteristics of under-populated countries
Assess the positive impacts of underpopulation on resource use
Assess the negative impacts, including workforce shortage and aging population
g9-geography-ug6-t4.simple: Underpopulation exists when a population is too small to utilize its resources fully, or when the resources could support a larger population without lowering living standards or raising unemployment. Under-populated areas today are usually large in area and rich in resources; they can export surplus food, energy and minerals and enjoy high incomes, good living conditions, advanced technology and immigration. Fewer people means lower demand for resources, so resource depletion and environmental impacts fall. But underpopulation also brings fewer workers, so resource production declines; populations age, taxes shrink and the demand for services falls with growth.
g9-geography-ug6-t4.detailed:
Definition. Under population may be said to exist where a population is too small to utilize fully its resources, or where the resources could support a larger population without lowering living standards or increasing unemployment. The first meaning - too few people to use the resources - is more frequent than the second. Simply put, underpopulation is when there are more resources in an area (food, energy, minerals) than can be used by the people living there, and when a region has insufficient workers to exploit its resources efficiently, support its retired population and provide growth. The resources are vast and much can be produced, but people are not sufficient.

Absolute and relative under-population. Absolute under population is quite rare, occurring only in isolated populations whose numbers cannot achieve normal demographic replacement or adequate economic production. Relative under-population occurs where there is insufficient development of the resources available; nowhere is it more common than in the southern continents.

Character portraits of under-populated lands. Most areas considered under-populated today are large in area and rich in resources. These countries can export surpluses of food, energy and mineral resources, and they have high incomes, good living conditions, a good level of technology and immigration inflows. This phenomenon results in a decline in population, and with fewer people there is a decrease in the demand for services.

Positive impacts on resource use. The advantages include a decrease in resource demand, which leads to reduced resource depletion and lower environmental impacts: forests, water and minerals are drawn on more slowly, so ecosystems face less strain.

Negative impacts on development. On the other hand, with fewer people the demand for resources such as food, water and energy decreases, which also leads to a decline in resource production because there are fewer workers in the industries that produce them. Underpopulation can lead to aging populations and a declining workforce, which further deepens the fall in production. It also brings a shortage of workforce and fewer people to pay taxes, weakening public services even as the demand for services itself declines.

keyTerms.def: A condition where the population is too small to utilize fully the resources of its area.
The rare case of an isolated population too small for normal demographic replacement or adequate production.
Underpopulation caused by insufficient development of available resources; common in the southern continents.
The broadly less-developed continents of the southern hemisphere used in the textbook to locate relative under-population.
A rising share of older people in a population, typical of prolonged underpopulation.
Too few working people to farm, mine, build and staff industries efficiently.
The capacity of a population to renew its numbers across generations.

workedExamples.problem: A large country has fertile land, abundant minerals and energy, yet much of its farmland lies unused and mines stand idle because of a lack of workers. Identify the population concept and justify it.
workedExamples.given: Resources exceed what the resident population can use; production limited by labor supply.
workedExamples.formula: Concept: underpopulation exists where people are too few to utilize resources fully.
workedExamples.substitution: Resources vast, much could be produced, but workers are not sufficient.
workedExamples.calculation: Since the constraint is the number of people rather than the quantity of resources, the country sits below its optimal population size.
workedExamples.answer: This is underpopulation: resources outstrip the population able to use them.

workedExamples.problem: A resource-rich country has neither labor shortage overstressing the land nor unemployment - but a planning ministry needs to know why its natural increase is negative yet living standards hold. Which textbook clause explains it?
workedExamples.given: The population is smaller than the resources could support; living standards remain high and unemployment has not increased.
workedExamples.formula: Concept: resources could support a larger population without lowering living standards or increasing unemployment.
workedExamples.substitution: Even if the population grew, both living standards and employment would be maintained.
workedExamples.calculation: Adding people would raise output and tax revenue without stretching the resource base, so the balance still favors growth.
workedExamples.answer: The country is under-populated because its resources can carry a larger population harmlessly.

workedExamples.problem: Two effects of underpopulation are listed: lower environmental impact and declining resource production. Explain why both follow from the same cause.
workedExamples.given: Fewer people means lower demand for food, water and energy.
workedExamples.formula: Concept: population size drives both demand for and supply of resources.
workedExamples.substitution: Low demand reduces extraction and pollution; the same small workforce reduces production of food, water and energy.
workedExamples.calculation: The single cause - few people - acts twice: consumption pressure falls, but so does the labor available to produce and pay for services.
workedExamples.answer: Fewer people reduce depletion and pollution, but they also shrink production and the tax base - the benefit and the cost have one root.

workedExamples.problem: Why does the textbook locate relative under-population most commonly in the southern continents? Reason from the definition.
workedExamples.given: Relative under-population is insufficient development of the resources available.
workedExamples.formula: Concept: resources minus their development equals latent abundance unused.
workedExamples.substitution: Southern continents hold large, rich areas whose resources are under-developed rather than exhausted.
workedExamples.calculation: Where resources are plentiful but under-developed, the population cannot fully use them with current technology and investment, producing relative under-population.
workedExamples.answer: Rich but under-developed resources leave the populations of the southern continents too few in effect to exploit them.

commonMistakes: Believing underpopulation means simply a small population in a small country; the emphasis is on resources remaining unused.
Confusing underpopulation with low population density in infertile deserts or tundra that cannot support many people anyway.
Thinking underpopulation is purely positive; it also causes workforce shortage, aging and lower tax revenue.
Assuming absolute underpopulation is widespread; the textbook says it is quite rare.
Forgetting that relative under-population means the problem is under-development of resources, not lack of resources.
Ignoring that under-populated countries often import workers through immigration.
applications: Listing countries commonly described as under-populated and comparing their resource wealth.
Predicting how an aging, shrinking workforce slows farming and mining output.
Discussing why emigration from Ethiopia, if it lowered the population far below resources, would also cut labor and taxes.
Comparing under-populated exporters of food and minerals with over-populated importers.
Explaining why the demand for schools and clinics falls when population declines, and why that is not always good news.
g9-geography-ug6-t4.summary: Underpopulation exists when people are too few to use their resources fully or when resources could carry a larger population without loss of living standards. Its absolute form is rare; the relative form, from under-development of resources, is most common in the southern continents. Fewer people ease environmental pressure but shrink the workforce, production, tax revenue and services.

pairs.q: State the two textbook definitions of underpopulation.
pairs.a: Too small a population to use resources fully; resources could support more people without lower living standards or higher unemployment.

pairs.q: Where is relative under-population most common?
Name two traits of under-populated lands.
pairs.a: Large area, rich resources, emigrants welcome, high incomes and technology.

g9-geography-ug6-t5.overview: Rapid population growth strains Ethiopia's land, forests, water and air. This lesson quantifies deforestation, pollution and land degradation in Ethiopia and links them to its fast-growing population.
objectives: Assess the impacts of rapid population growth on the environment
Quantify the historical decline of forest cover in Ethiopia
Explain how population growth causes pollution in urban and rural areas
Describe land and soil degradation and locate its hotspots
Evaluate the consequences for crop productivity and farming systems
g9-geography-ug6-t5.simple: Rapid population growth places incredible strain on the environment. Ethiopia's population exceeded 101 million by 2016 and grows at about 2.6 percent per year - faster than the economy - pressing beyond the carrying capacity of land, water, soil and forest. Deforestation is the clearest impact: high forests may once have covered 35-40 percent of the land, 16 percent in the early 1950s, 3.6 percent in the early 1980s and only 2.7 percent by 1989, with 150,000-200,000 hectares lost yearly. Biomass supplies over 99 percent of domestic energy, and charcoal plus fuelwood demands keep climbing. Pollution hits cities and farms alike, and over 85 percent of land is degraded, with hotspots in Tigray, Wollo and Gondar.
g9-geography-ug6-t5.detailed:
Population pressure in Ethiopia. Ethiopia's population was estimated at over 101 million by 2016 and continues to grow at 2.6 percent per year, a rate higher than the economic growth rate, so numbers grow beyond the carrying capacity of the country's natural resources such as land, water, soil and forest. Most people earn their livelihoods in lands now categorized as moderately to severely degraded, mostly in the Ethiopian highlands; without significant conservation measures, moderately degraded lands may become rigorously degraded.

Deforestation. Deforestation is the removal of forest cover without adequate replacement - the indiscriminate destruction of natural vegetation. Removing forests raises atmospheric carbon dioxide, disrupts the photosynthesis cycle that plants use to absorb carbon dioxide and release oxygen, and harms other species of biodiversity. In Ethiopia, deforestation follows people's growing needs for wood, agricultural land, settlement land and grazing land, and there is a direct correlation between population density and deforestation: the more people in an area, the more trees they cut. Historical sources suggest high forests might once have covered 35-40 percent of the land, and 66 percent with savanna woodlands included.

Measuring the decline. High forests covered 16 percent of the land in the early 1950s, 3.6 percent in the early 1980s, and only 2.7 percent in 1989; with about five million hectares of savanna woodlands then remaining, total forest and woody vegetation stood at about 7 percent, falling to less than 2.7 percent by 1994. At the current annual loss of 150,000-200,000 hectares of high forest, only scattered minor stands may survive in inaccessible areas within a few decades.

Energy dependence. Biomass energy offers over 99 percent of total domestic energy consumption, 92 percent for households and the rest for small-scale industry and food enterprises; about 78 percent is woody biomass, 12 percent animal dung and 9 percent crop residue. Over the last 50 years charcoal production rose from one million to more than three million tons per year, and fuelwood consumption rose from 40 to 100 million cubic meters per year - all at the expense of forests. Where fuelwood grows scarce, dung and crop residues are burned instead of being recycled into the soil, draining soil nutrients and organic matter.

Pollution. In Ethiopia, agriculture is the major source of pollution: chemical fertilizers and pesticides contaminate soil, water and living organisms. Indoor air pollution from biomass fuel is responsible for 50,320 annual deaths of children under five, about 4.9 percent of the national burden of disease. In cities like Addis Ababa, inhabitants face polluted air and water from garbage, households, industries, automobiles and unmanaged open landfills; many leather processing industries lack proper waste treatment, releasing salt, pesticides, flesh, hair, sulfates, ammonia and acids into water bodies.

Land and soil degradation. Land degradation involves soil erosion and loss of soil fertility. Ethiopia's high-intensity rainstorms and steep slopes make it highly susceptible to erosion, especially in the highlands; a 1 percent increase in soil organic matter reduces erodibility by about 15 percent. Over 85 percent of the land is moderately to very severely degraded and about 75 percent is affected by desertification; satellite imagery over the last three decades shows degradation hotspots covering about 23 percent of the land area, largely in Tigray, Wollo and Gondar. As vegetative cover is removed for crops, grazing and fuel, surface runoff rises, nutrients and water-holding capacity fall, cropland reverts to grassland and finally to bare rock, and the vicious cycle of degradation reinforces itself.

keyTerms.def: Removal of forest cover without adequate replacement; the indiscriminate destruction of natural vegetation.
Population increase of about 2.6 percent per year in Ethiopia, outpacing economic growth.
The decline in quality of a resource; land degradation includes soil erosion and loss of fertility.
Any undesirable change in natural conditions of air, water or other environment that harms health and activities.
Energy from wood, dung and crop residues; over 99 percent of Ethiopia's domestic energy consumption.
The combined return of water to the atmosphere by plants and soil; deforestation reduces it, affecting rainfall.
The process by which productive land becomes desert-like; about 75 percent of Ethiopia's land is affected.
How easily soil is eroded; falls about 15 percent for each 1 percent rise in soil organic matter.

workedExamples.problem: Ethiopia's high forest cover was 16 percent in the early 1950s and 2.7 percent in 1989. By what relative share did the cover decline over that period?
workedExamples.given: Cover in early 1950s: 16 percent of land area. Cover in 1989: 2.7 percent.
workedExamples.formula: Method: divide the later value by the earlier value to find the remaining fraction of the original.
workedExamples.substitution: 2.7 / 16 = 0.169, so less than 17 percent of the early 1950s cover remained.
workedExamples.calculation: About 83 percent of the remaining high forest was lost within roughly four decades, and by 1994 the figure had fallen again below 2.7 percent.
workedExamples.answer: High forest cover fell to less than a fifth of its 1950s extent - a loss of about 83 percent of what remained of the original forests.

workedExamples.problem: At the current annual loss of 150,000-200,000 hectares of high forest, what does the textbook project for the coming decades?
workedExamples.given: Annual loss: 150,000-200,000 hectares; remaining high forests are already scattered.
workedExamples.formula: Concept: cumulative loss over decades equals annual loss multiplied by the number of years.
workedExamples.substitution: 150,000 ha x 10 years = 1,500,000 ha; 200,000 ha x 10 years = 2,000,000 ha per decade.
workedExamples.calculation: Repeating this decade after decade exhausts remaining accessible stands, so the textbook projects only scattered minor stands of heavily disturbed forests in inaccessible parts within a few decades.
workedExamples.answer: High forests may be reduced to scattered minor stands in inaccessible parts of the country within a few decades.

workedExamples.problem: Biomass energy supplies over 99 percent of Ethiopia's domestic energy: 78 percent woody biomass, 12 percent animal dung, 9 percent crop residue. What does this composition mean for land degradation?
workedExamples.given: Total domestic energy share: over 99 percent biomass; composition 78 percent wood, 12 percent dung, 9 percent crop residue.
workedExamples.formula: Concept: household energy choices transfer nutrients from farm fields to fires.
workedExamples.substitution: Wood burning drives deforestation; dung and residue burning removes nutrients that should be recycled into the soil.
workedExamples.calculation: Since dung already largely replaces wood as household fuel in the intensively farmed and degraded north and east, soil loses nutrients and organic matter, cutting crop productivity and resistance to drought.
workedExamples.answer: Heavy biomass dependence links household cooking directly to deforestation and nutrient loss, deepening the degradation cycle.

workedExamples.problem: Ethiopia grows at 2.6 percent per year while its economic growth lags behind. Why does the textbook call the result a threat to resources?
workedExamples.given: Population over 101 million (2016), 2.6 percent annual growth, growth exceeding economic growth rate.
workedExamples.formula: Concept: population growth beyond carrying capacity of land, water, soil and forest degrades them.
workedExamples.substitution: Demand for food, fuel, farmland and housing rises about 2.6 percent yearly while production capacity grows more slowly.
workedExamples.calculation: The widening gap forces over-exploitation: forest clearing, overgrazing, erosion and pollution across moderately to severely degraded lands, especially in the highlands.
workedExamples.answer: Because growth exceeds both the economy and the carrying capacity of resources, over-exploitation and environmental degradation intensify each year.

commonMistakes: Confusing deforestation in size with degradation in quality; the textbook says forests declined both in size and quality.
Believing Ethiopia's forest loss happened only recently; the sharpest fall occurred between the 1950s and the 1980s.
Attributing pollution only to factories; the textbook names agriculture as the major source of environmental pollution.
Thinking charcoal and fuelwood figures are small; charcoal tripled and fuelwood multiplied 2.5 times in 50 years.
Forgetting that burning dung and crop residues steals nutrients from the soil, not just trees from the forest.
Assuming degradation is uniform across Ethiopia; hotspots concentrate in Tigray, Wollo and Gondar.
applications: Using the forest figures (16 percent, 3.6 percent, 2.7 percent) to sketch a decline graph of Ethiopian forests.
Explaining why conservation measures must target moderately degraded highlands before they become rigorously degraded.
Investigating how households in your area cook: wood, dung, charcoal or kerosene, and what that means for nearby land.
Debating the impact of rapid growth on housing, education, food supply, health care, farmland and drought.
Proposing local actions such as tree planting, terracing or improved stoves to break the degradation cycle.
g9-geography-ug6-t5.summary: Ethiopia's 101-million-plus population growing at 2.6 percent per year exceeds the carrying capacity of its resources, driving deforestation from 16 percent forest cover in the early 1950s to 2.7 percent by 1989, pollution led by agriculture and urban centers, and land degradation affecting over 85 percent of the land. Biomass dependence, burning 150,000-200,000 hectares of forest worth of wood yearly, ties household energy directly to the vicious cycle of degradation.
